title: Peak Performance Gym: forecasting next year's results with a trend model for a bank loan
participant_role: Financial analyst helping a gym prepare a budget for a bank loan application
judge_role: Owner of Peak Performance Gym, who is preparing next year's budget for a bank loan application

difficulty.rationale: Plug numbers into a given regression and project income; easier than ICDC.
difficulty.suggested_adjustment: Add a capacity or pricing decision to raise it to ICDC.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a financial analyst hired by PEAK PERFORMANCE GYM. The owner (judge) wants your help preparing next year's budget, which will be part of a loan application to a local bank.

PEAK PERFORMANCE GYM has been open for five years and has grown every year. The owner (judge) wants to borrow money to buy new equipment, and the bank has asked for a projection of next year's (year 6) revenue, expenses and operating income, with an explanation of how the projection was made. Until now the owner (judge) has budgeted by "adding a little to last year," and the owner (judge) is not sure that approach will satisfy a bank loan officer.

You exported the year end membership counts from the gym's membership software and ran a trend regression in a spreadsheet. You also gathered the gym's revenue and cost information from the accounting records.

[Membership history and regression output: see exhibits]

[Revenue and cost information: see exhibits]

The owner (judge) wants a clear, believable forecast to hand the bank, an understanding of how the forecast was built and what could go wrong, and advice on how the gym's systems can make forecasting easier in the future.

You must:
- Identify the types of data analysis modeling techniques the gym could use for its forecast
- Apply the regression model to project year 6 membership
- Project year 6 revenue, expenses and operating income
- Prepare a pessimistic scenario and explain what it means for the loan application
- Explain the role of financial-information management and technology in building the forecast

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's office at the gym. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Can I just use the optimistic number for the bank?
What if our gym can only hold 650 members?

solution.overview: A strong answer names the main modeling techniques (trend or time series, regression, scenario or sensitivity analysis, simulation), applies the regression to project 694 members in year 6, and builds a projection of $416,400 revenue, $83,280 variable costs, $185,400 fixed costs and $147,720 operating income. A pessimistic case with 10% fewer members (625) still earns $114,600. The presenter explains that R squared of 0.99 shows a close fit to the past but not a guarantee, recommends giving the bank a range, and explains how financial-information management and technology (spreadsheets, BI dashboards, membership software linked to accounting) support the forecast.

answer: Trend or time series analysis: uses past patterns over time to project the future
Regression: finds the line that best fits the data (here, members by year)
Scenario or sensitivity analysis: tests best case, expected and worst case assumptions
Simulation: runs many possible outcomes to show a range of results
Model: Members = 346 + 58 x Year, so the gym adds about 58 members a year
R squared of 0.99 means the trend line fits the past five years very closely
A close fit to the past is not a guarantee: competition, capacity or the economy could change the trend

by_task.task: Projected revenue, expenses and operating income
answer: Variable costs: 694 x $120 = $83,280
Operating income: 416,400 minus 83,280 minus 185,400 = $147,720
10% fewer members: 694 x 0.9 = 624.6, rounded to 625 members
Revenue $375,000, variable costs $75,000, fixed costs $185,400
Operating income $114,600, still clearly profitable
Showing the bank a range builds credibility and shows the loan can be repaid even in a weaker year
Financial-information management collects, processes, stores and reports financial data so managers can make decisions
It ensures the forecast uses accurate, consistent data from the accounting and membership records
Spreadsheet functions such as TREND, FORECAST and LINEST run the regression quickly
Membership software feeding the accounting system and BI dashboards let the owner compare actual results with the budget each month

calculations.label: Capacity limit check (judge question)
steps: If the gym can hold only 650 members, revenue is capped at 650 x 600 = $390,000

judge_question_answers.question: Can I just use the optimistic number for the bank?
answer: No: presenting only the most favorable number would be misleading and could damage your credibility
Banks see many forecasts and will test your assumptions
Show the expected case with a pessimistic case (and a range) and explain the method
An honest range that still covers the loan payments is more convincing than one rosy number

judge_question_answers.question: What if our gym can only hold 650 members?
answer: Then the forecast of 694 members is not possible, so the model must be adjusted
At 650 members, revenue is capped at 650 x $600 = $390,000
A regression trend does not know about physical limits, so the analyst must add them
Growth beyond that would require raising prices, adding hours or expanding the space, which the loan could fund

key_concepts.definition: Using mathematical or statistical methods to describe past data and project future results.
Studying how a value changes over time to project where it is heading.
A method that finds the straight line that best fits the data, written as y = intercept + slope x X.
How much the predicted value changes for each one unit increase in the input; here about 58 members per year.
A measure from 0 to 1 of how well a model fits past data. A value near 1 means a very close fit, not a guaranteed future.
Preparing expected, pessimistic and optimistic versions of a forecast to show a range of outcomes.
Costs that change in total with activity, such as towels and app fees per member.
Costs that stay the same in total regardless of activity, such as rent and salaries.
Revenue minus variable and fixed operating costs; the profit from running the business.
The function that collects, processes, stores and reports financial data for decision making.
Software that gathers data from business systems and displays key results and trends visually.

notes: ICDC level because students must combine a regression model, a full revenue and expense projection and a scenario, then explain the information systems behind it. Watch for students who forget the 3% fixed cost increase, who treat R squared as proof the forecast will come true, or who suggest giving the bank only the optimistic number.

items.label: Identify types of data analysis modeling techniques

criteria.exceeds: Names and explains trend or time series analysis, regression, scenario or sensitivity analysis and simulation, and explains why a regression based trend with scenarios is stronger for a bank than "adding a little to last year."
criteria.meets: Identifies at least trend or time series analysis, regression and scenario analysis and briefly explains what each does.
criteria.below: Names one or two techniques without explaining them, or cannot say why they are better than the owner's current approach.
criteria.little: Does not identify any modeling techniques.

items.label: Apply mathematical data analysis modeling techniques

criteria.exceeds: Applies Members = 346 + 58 x Year to project 694 members in year 6 (about 58 new members a year), explains that R squared of 0.99 shows a very close fit to the past, and cautions that it is not a guarantee because competition, capacity or the economy could change the trend.
criteria.meets: Correctly projects 694 members in year 6 using the regression and explains that R squared of 0.99 means the line fits the past data closely.
criteria.below: Makes an error applying the model (for example using year 5 or misreading the slope), or treats R squared as proof the forecast will come true.
criteria.little: Does not apply the regression, or produces a membership number unrelated to the model.

criteria.exceeds: Projects revenue of $416,400, variable costs of $83,280, fixed costs of $185,400 (3% increase) and operating income of $147,720, then builds a pessimistic case of 625 members with operating income of $114,600 and explains that showing the bank this range proves the loan can be repaid in a weaker year.
criteria.meets: Projects revenue of $416,400, variable costs of $83,280, fixed costs of $185,400 and operating income of $147,720, and prepares the pessimistic case of $114,600.
criteria.below: Forgets the 3% fixed cost increase (using $180,000), makes a calculation error, or omits the pessimistic scenario.
criteria.little: Does not project revenue, expenses or operating income.

items.label: Explain the nature and scope of the financial-information management function

criteria.exceeds: Explains that financial-information management collects, processes, stores and reports financial data for decisions, and that it keeps the forecast built on accurate, consistent data from the membership and accounting records, which gives the bank confidence in the numbers.
criteria.meets: Explains that financial-information management collects and reports financial data so managers can make decisions, and that accurate records support the forecast.
criteria.below: Describes financial-information management vaguely, or does not connect it to the forecast.
criteria.little: Does not explain the financial-information management function.

items.label: Describe the use of technology in the financial-information management function

criteria.exceeds: Describes spreadsheet functions such as TREND, FORECAST and LINEST to run the regression, membership software that feeds the accounting system, and BI dashboards that let the owner compare actual results with the budget each month.
criteria.meets: Describes how spreadsheets run the regression and how linked membership and accounting software or dashboards make forecasting easier.
criteria.below: Mentions technology in general terms without explaining how it helps the gym forecast.
criteria.little: Does not describe any use of technology.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the membership trend to revenue, costs and operating income, and recognizes limits the model cannot see, such as the gym's capacity.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the regression and cost data to the projected operating income.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or trusts the model without question.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Recommends giving the bank the expected case, the pessimistic case and an explanation of the method, and suggests how the owner can track actual results against the budget.
criteria.meets: Recommends presenting the bank with a range rather than a single number.
criteria.below: Gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or suggests giving the bank only the optimistic number.

criteria.exceeds: Explains the regression, R squared and the projection in plain language the owner could repeat to a loan officer, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the forecast and its method clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a simple visual such as a trend line chart or a side by side expected and pessimistic projection ($147,720 versus $114,600), and adds ideas such as a monthly budget dashboard.
criteria.meets: Organizes the forecast in a way that makes it easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions confidently: using only the optimistic number would be misleading, and an honest range that still covers the loan payments is more convincing; and with a 650 member limit the 694 forecast is impossible, revenue is capped at $390,000, and growth would need higher prices, more hours or more space, which the loan could fund.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the bank should see a range and that a 650 member cap limits revenue to $390,000.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees to give the bank only the optimistic number.

key_points: Modeling techniques include trend or time series analysis, regression, scenario or sensitivity analysis and simulation
Year 6 members = 346 + 58 x 6 = 694; R squared of 0.99 shows a close fit to the past but is not a guarantee
Expected case: revenue $416,400, variable costs $83,280, fixed costs $185,400 ($180,000 x 1.03), operating income $147,720
Pessimistic case: 625 members, revenue $375,000, variable costs $75,000, operating income $114,600
Give the bank a range with the method explained, not just the optimistic number
A 650 member capacity limit would cap revenue at $390,000
Spreadsheets (TREND, FORECAST, LINEST), linked membership and accounting software, and BI dashboards support forecasting
